pages.title: Surviving the fault: heat and breaking capacity
pages.for: A fault heats every conductor it flows through until the device opens. Check that the cpc and the live conductors can take that heat. Check that each device can break the biggest fault where it sits. If it cannot, a device upstream must.
pages.rule:
Fault current for the heat check = Uo × Cmax ÷ Zs, with Cmax 1.1
cpc: the size fitted must be at least S = √(I² × t) ÷ k
Live conductors: Zs(l/n) = Ze(l/n) + (R1+Rn), with Ze(l/n) = 230 ÷ PSCC
Then t = k² × S² ÷ I² must be longer than the device takes
Breaking capacity: IPF ≤ Icn, with IPF the larger of PEFC and PSCC
On a three-phase board, IPF is the three-line fault, about twice the line-to-neutral figure.

t is the device's time at that current, not the 0.4 s or 5 s allowed. The sum holds up to 5 s.
k: 115 for 70 °C thermoplastic copper, 143 for 90 °C thermosetting. Steel armour is far lower.
SWA armour may be the cpc if a calculation justifies it.

traps.text: Using the Cmin current for the heat check. It is the smaller current, so it gives too little heat.
Putting the 0.4 s or 5 s limit in for t. Use the device's time at that current.
Using copper's k for steel armour.
traps.cite: Slides p.59 (Tables 54.2 to 54.6); TMUK adiabatic calculator, in research

traps.text: Checking Icn against one line to earth when the three-phase fault is bigger.
Taking Table 54.7's cpc as proven. A suitable cpc and the minimum cpc are not the same thing.

pages.where: BS 7671 Regulations 434.5.1, 434.5.2 and 543.1.3. Tables 43.1 and 54.2 to 54.7. The device maker's data for Icn and let-through energy.

pages.name: Do you still have it?
pages.task: A circuit's Zs is 0.50 Ω. Which fault current do you put into S = √(I²t) ÷ k to check its cpc can take the heat?
pages.why: 230 × 1.1 ÷ 0.50 = 506.00 A. The supply can rise to 253 V, and more current means more heat.
pages.alt: 230 × 1.1 ÷ 0.50 = 506.00 A The supply can rise to 253 V. More voltage pushes more current round the same loop, and more current means more heat. 437.00 A is the Cmin current. That one is for whether the breaker opens in time. 460.00 A leaves out Cmax. It misses the rise to 253 V.
pages.html:
230 × 1.1 ÷ 0.50 = 506.00 A

The supply can rise to 253 V. More voltage pushes more current round the same loop, and more current means more heat.

437.00 A is the Cmin current. That one is for whether the breaker opens in time.

460.00 A leaves out Cmax. It misses the rise to 253 V.

pages.name: What it is for
pages.text:
A fault current heats every conductor it flows through until the device opens. A fault that clears quickly gives the heat no time to leave. Copper that gets too hot damages its insulation.

So three checks follow Zs. The cpc must take the heat of an earth fault. The live conductors must take the heat of a short circuit. And each device must be able to break the biggest fault where it sits. A device may be rated lower only if one upstream can break that fault for it.
pages.alt: A fault current heats every conductor it flows through until the device opens. A fault that clears quickly gives the heat no time to leave. Copper that gets too hot damages its insulation. So three checks follow Zs. The cpc must take the heat of an earth fault. The live conductors must take the heat of a short circuit. And each device must be able to break the biggest fault where it sits. A device may be rated lower only if one upstream can break that fault for it. If it is skipped: A cpc that passes on Zs can still get hot enough to damage its insulation before the breaker opens.
pages.html:
A fault current heats every conductor it flows through until the device opens. A fault that clears quickly gives the heat no time to leave. Copper that gets too hot damages its insulation.

So three checks follow Zs. The cpc must take the heat of an earth fault. The live conductors must take the heat of a short circuit. And each device must be able to break the biggest fault where it sits. A device may be rated lower only if one upstream can break that fault for it.

If it is skipped: A cpc that passes on Zs can still get hot enough to damage its insulation before the breaker opens. A device asked to break more current than it is rated for may destroy itself.

pages.name: The why
pages.text: At 0.646 Ω the Cmax current is 391.64 A. The cpc needs 1.08 mm², so 1.5 mm² holds. At 0.43 Ω the Cmin current asks for 1.40 mm², a pass. The Cmax current asks for 1.62 mm², a fail. This takes the breaker's time as 0.1 s. Close to the board it opens faster, so check the maker's let-through figure there.
pages.alt: Heat put in during 0.1 s: I² × 0.1 What 1.5 mm² can take: k²S² Cmax current: the right-hand dot Cmin current: the left-hand dot This takes the breaker's time as 0.1 s. Close to the board it opens faster, so check the maker's let-through figure there. Fault current at Cmin 508.14 A Fault current at Cmax 588.37 A Smallest cpc, at Cmax 1.62 mm² SMALLEST CPC THAT COPES AT THE CMAX CURRENT 1.5 mm² fitted At Cmax, 588.37 A puts 34618 A²s into the cpc. That is more than 1.5 mm² can take, so it needs 1.62 mm². The Cmin dot is still under the line. A check at Cmin would pass this cpc wrongly.
pages.html:
Heat put in during 0.1 s: I² × 0.1What 1.5 mm² can take: k²S²
Cmax current: the right-hand dotCmin current: the left-hand dot

This takes the breaker's time as 0.1 s. Close to the board it opens faster, so check the maker's let-through figure there.

Fault current at Cmin508.14 A
Fault current at Cmax588.37 A
Smallest cpc, at Cmax1.62 mm²
Smallest cpc that copes at the Cmax current

At Cmax, 588.37 A puts 34618 A²s into the cpc. That is more than 1.5 mm² can take, so it needs 1.62 mm². The Cmin dot is still under the line. A check at Cmin would pass this cpc wrongly.

A fault heats the copper faster than the heat can leave it. So the heat stays in the conductor while the fault lasts. The heat is I² × R × t. Halve the area and the resistance doubles, with half the copper to warm. So the temperature climbs four times as fast. That is why the area is squared.

k sums up the copper, the insulation, the temperature it starts at and the temperature it must not pass. The conductor survives if the fault's I²t is no more than k²S². Turn that round and the smallest area is S = √(I²t) ÷ k.

Lesson 6 wanted the smallest current, to be sure the breaker opens in time. The heat check wants the largest, because more current puts in more heat in the same 0.1 s. One Zs, two currents, two questions. Turn the same sum round and you get how long the live conductors last in a short circuit: t = k²S² ÷ I². If that is longer than the device takes, the cable holds out.

pages.name: Check
pages.task: A 32 A type C breaker protects a circuit with Zs 0.38 Ω. Its cpc is 2.5 mm² in 70 °C thermoplastic cable, so k is 115. It is a final circuit, so 0.4 s is allowed. At the Cmax current, 665.79 A, the breaker opens within 0.1 s. What is the smallest cpc that copes?
pages.answer: 1.83 mm²: the Cmax current for 0.1 s
pages.alt: t is how long the device takes at that current. √(665.79² × 0.1) ÷ 115 = 1.83 mm², so the 2.5 mm² cpc holds.
options: 1.83 mm²: the Cmax current for 0.1 s
3.66 mm²: the Cmax current for 0.4 s
1.58 mm²: the Cmin current for 0.1 s
pages.html: t is how long the device takes at that current. √(665.79² × 0.1) ÷ 115 = 1.83 mm², so the 2.5 mm² cpc holds.

pages.name: Worked example
pages.text: The heater's Cmax current is 391.64 A. Its cpc needs 1.08 mm², under the 1.5 mm² fitted. In the short circuit the greatest current is 203.87 A. The 2.5 mm² conductors can carry it for 3.08 s, far longer than the 0.1 s the RCBO takes.
pages.alt: FIRST, THE HEATER'S CPC FROM LESSON 6 15 m of 1.5 mm² 70 °C thermoplastic singles in conduit, with a 1.5 mm² cpc. A 16 A type B breaker. Zs is 0.646 Ω. Cmin current = 230 × 0.95 ÷ 0.646 = 338.24 A. That is over the breaker's Ia, 80 A, so it opens within 0.1 s. Cmax current = 230 × 1.1 ÷ 0.646 = 391.64 A. The breaker still opens within 0.1 s. k for the cpc is 115. S = √(391.64² × 0.1) ÷ 115 = 1.08 mm². That is under 1.5 mm², so the cpc holds. SECOND, A SHORT CIRCUIT ON THE LIVE CONDUCTORS A single-phase circuit in 2.5 mm² twin and earth, 90 °C thermosetting, with a 1.5 mm² cpc. It runs 25 m.
pages.html:
First, the heater's cpc from lesson 6

15 m of 1.5 mm² 70 °C thermoplastic singles in conduit, with a 1.5 mm² cpc. A 16 A type B breaker. Zs is 0.646 Ω.

Cmin current = 230 × 0.95 ÷ 0.646 = 338.24 A. That is over the breaker's Ia, 80 A, so it opens within 0.1 s.

Cmax current = 230 × 1.1 ÷ 0.646 = 391.64 A. The breaker still opens within 0.1 s.

k for the cpc is 115. S = √(391.64² × 0.1) ÷ 115 = 1.08 mm².

That is under 1.5 mm², so the cpc holds.

Second, a short circuit on the live conductors

A single-phase circuit in 2.5 mm² twin and earth, 90 °C thermosetting, with a 1.5 mm² cpc. It runs 25 m. A 20 A RCBO protects it, opening within 0.1 s at 100 A. The short-circuit current at the origin is measured as 300 A.

Ze(l/n) = 230 ÷ 300 = 0.767 Ω. That is the supply's own loop, line to neutral.

R1+Rn = 14.82 × 1.28 × 25 ÷ 1000 = 0.474 Ω

Zs(l/n) = 0.767 + 0.474 = 1.241 Ω

Least current = 230 × 0.95 ÷ 1.241 = 176.07 A. That is over 100 A, so the RCBO opens within 0.1 s.

Greatest current = 230 × 1.1 ÷ 1.241 = 203.87 A

k for 90 °C thermosetting copper is 143. t = 143² × 2.5² ÷ 203.87² = 3.08 s.

The conductors can carry it for 3.08 s. The RCBO opens within 0.1 s. So they are safe.

Your notes may show 341.4 A and 395.3 A for the heater. They come from Zs cut to 0.64 Ω. The cpc still passes. For the short circuit they may show 177.6 A, 205.6 A and 3.02 s. They come from Zs(l/n) worked as 1.23 Ω. The conductors still pass.

(c) Determine, for the motor circuit, whether the copper circuit protective conductor satisfies the thermal constraints under fault conditions. First, the minimum cpc size.

The motor circuit's cpc is 2.5 mm². It runs in the same conduit as the 90 °C thermosetting singles, so k is 143. Take Zs at DBP2 as 0.15 Ω for practice. Zs at the starter is then 0.366 Ω.

First, the minimum cpc size.

Cmax current = 230 × 1.1 ÷ 0.366 = 691.26 A

That is past 250 A, so the 25 A type C opens within 0.1 s.

S = √(691.26² × 0.1) ÷ 143 = 1.53 mm² ≤ 2.5 mm²: satisfies

1.53 mm² is under the 2.5 mm² fitted, so the cpc satisfies the thermal constraints.

Take the starter-to-motor leg as 3.0 m for practice. Zs at the motor is then 0.459 Ω. 230 × 1.1 ÷ 0.459 = 551.20 A, so S = √(551.20² × 0.1) ÷ 143 = 1.22 mm². Its 1.5 mm² cpc holds too. The 25 A breaker at DBP2 guards this smaller leg against fault current. That works because the leg can take the fault's heat. Regulation 434.2.1 sets the conditions for a device placed upstream of a step down in size.

pages.name: Section A 2(e)
pages.task: Every device must break the biggest fault current where it sits. That current is IPF, the larger of the earth fault current and the short-circuit current. The device's breaking capacity, Icn, is marked on it, usually in a small box. The rule is IPF ≤ Icn. The showroom's supply has Ze 0.1 Ω. Its stated fault current is 4.6 kA. (e) Determine the least rated short-circuit breaking capacity (Icn) for the circuit-breakers in the MDB.
pages.alt: CARRIED FORWARD (c) Section A 2(c): minimum cpc for the motor circuit, thermal constraints 1.53 mm² Every device must break the biggest fault current where it sits. That current is IPF, the larger of the earth fault current and the short-circuit current. The device's breaking capacity, Icn, is marked on it, usually in a small box. The rule is IPF ≤ Icn. The showroom's supply has Ze 0.1 Ω. Its stated fault current is 4.6 kA. IPF = 4.6 kA at the origin Icn ≥ 4.6 kA Take the stated 4.6 kA as a fault across all three lines at the origin. That is the biggest fault there, so it sets Icn.
pages.html:
Carried forward
(c)Section A 2(c): minimum cpc for the motor circuit, thermal constraints1.53 mm²

Every device must break the biggest fault current where it sits. That current is IPF, the larger of the earth fault current and the short-circuit current. The device's breaking capacity, Icn, is marked on it, usually in a small box. The rule is IPF ≤ Icn.

The showroom's supply has Ze 0.1 Ω. Its stated fault current is 4.6 kA.

IPF = 4.6 kA at the origin

Icn ≥ 4.6 kA

Take the stated 4.6 kA as a fault across all three lines at the origin. That is the biggest fault there, so it sets Icn. A breaker marked 6 kA passes. One marked 4.5 kA does not.

Why is 4.6 kA about twice 230 ÷ 0.1? In a fault across all three lines, the neutral carries no current. So the fault current meets one line's impedance, not a line and a return. That roughly halves the loop and doubles the current. A common rule of thumb simply doubles the line-neutral figure. That rule overstates the real current. For Icn, that is the safe way round.

A lower Icn is allowed only where a device on the supply side has the breaking capacity needed.

pages.task: SWA armour can be the cpc if a calculation justifies it. This is that calculation. Assume the DBL2 submain is four-core 4 mm² 90 °C thermosetting XLPE/SWA cable, 17.0 m on plan. A 10 A type C breaker at the MDB protects it. The armour is its cpc. Treat the cable size and the breaker as practice values. Lesson 8 sizes them properly. Each core is 4.61 mΩ/m and the armour 6.8 mΩ/m, both at 20 °C. The armour area is 22 mm². Use the 1.28 multiplier on both. Take k for the steel armour as 46 for practice. SWA armour can be the cpc if a calculation justifies it. This is that calculation.

Assume the DBL2 submain is four-core 4 mm² 90 °C thermosetting XLPE/SWA cable, 17.0 m on plan. A 10 A type C breaker at the MDB protects it. The armour is its cpc. Treat the cable size and the breaker as practice values. Lesson 8 sizes them properly.

Each core is 4.61 mΩ/m and the armour 6.8 mΩ/m, both at 20 °C. The armour area is 22 mm². Use the 1.28 multiplier on both.

Take k for the steel armour as 46 for practice. On a real job, read k from Table 54.4.

R1+R2 = (4.61 + 6.8) × 1.28 × 17.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.248 Ω

Zs at DBL2 = 0.1 + 0.248 = 0.348 Ω

Cmin current = 230 × 0.95 ÷ 0.348 = 627.87 A

That is far past 100 A, so the breaker opens within 0.1 s.

Cmax current = 230 × 1.1 ÷ 0.348 = 727.01 A

S = √(727.01² × 0.1) ÷ 46 = 5.00 mm² ≤ 22 mm²: justified

The armour is 22 mm², far more than 5.00 mm². So it is justified as the cpc.

As a cross-check, the armour is rated 1.0 kA for 1 s. The same I²t over 0.1 s is 1.0 × √10 = 3.16 kA, well above 727.01 A. Carry Zs at DBL2, 0.348 Ω, into lesson 8.

pages.name: Section B
pages.task: Explain the difference between a suitable cpc and a minimum cpc.
pages.why: A model answer: A suitable cpc is the size Table 54.7 gives from the line conductor. Below 16 mm² that is the same size as the line. The minimum cpc is the smallest size that still passes the heat check, S = √(I²t) ÷ k. It may be smaller than the suitable one. The heat check uses the largest fault current, at Cmax, the device's time at that current, and k for the cpc's material and insulation. To find the minimum, choose a smaller cpc and redo the steps from R1+R2 to the heat check. A smaller cpc raises R1+R2 and Zs. So Zs must still be within the device's maximum, and the fault current must still open it in time. If the smaller size fails the heat check, the size above it is the minimum.

pages.name: Changed numbers
pages.task: A single-phase circuit is wired in 4 mm² twin and earth, 90 °C thermosetting, 30 m long. A 32 A type B breaker protects it, opening within 0.1 s once the current reaches 160 A. The short-circuit current at the origin is 500 A. Use 9.22 mΩ/m for the line and neutral together, and the 1.28 multiplier. Determine whether the breaker protects the live conductors in a short circuit. First, how long can they carry the greatest short-circuit current?
pages.alt: A single-phase circuit is wired in 4 mm² twin and earth, 90 °C thermosetting, 30 m long. A 32 A type B breaker protects it, opening within 0.1 s once the current reaches 160 A. The short-circuit current at the origin is 500 A. Use 9.22 mΩ/m for the line and neutral together, and the 1.28 multiplier. First, how long can they carry the greatest short-circuit current? Ze(l/n) = 230 ÷ 500 = 0.460 Ω R1+Rn = 9.22 × 1.28 × 30 ÷ 1000 = 0.354 Ω Zs(l/n) = 0.460 + 0.354 = 0.814 Ω Least current = 230 × 0.95 ÷ 0.814 = 268.43 A That is over 160 A, so the breaker opens within 0.1 s.
pages.html:
A single-phase circuit is wired in 4 mm² twin and earth, 90 °C thermosetting, 30 m long. A 32 A type B breaker protects it, opening within 0.1 s once the current reaches 160 A. The short-circuit current at the origin is 500 A. Use 9.22 mΩ/m for the line and neutral together, and the 1.28 multiplier.

First, how long can they carry the greatest short-circuit current?

Ze(l/n) = 230 ÷ 500 = 0.460 Ω

R1+Rn = 9.22 × 1.28 × 30 ÷ 1000 = 0.354 Ω

Zs(l/n) = 0.460 + 0.354 = 0.814 Ω

Least current = 230 × 0.95 ÷ 0.814 = 268.43 A

That is over 160 A, so the breaker opens within 0.1 s.

Greatest current = 230 × 1.1 ÷ 0.814 = 310.81 A

t = 143² × 4² ÷ 310.81² = 3.39 s

3.39 s is far longer than the 0.1 s the breaker takes. So the live conductors are protected.
